questions.q: Your server starts without NODE_ENV set at all. Which environment does resolveEnvironment choose?
questions.explain: An unset NODE_ENV means development. That is why the one thing every production deployment must do is set NODE_ENV=production; otherwise development behaviour, such as full error details, switches on silently.
options: production, because it is on a server
development
test
It stops the app with an error

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: prod is an accepted alias for production. A missing value falls back to development, and staging is one of the four known environments.
options: production development staging
prod development staging
production production staging
production undefined staging

questions.q: Someone typed prodution. The app uses { strict: true }. What does this print?
questions.explain: Without strict a typo only warns and falls back to development, which is dangerous in production. With strict: true the typo throws, so the app stops at startup instead of running with the wrong behaviour.
options: startup stopped: bad NODE_ENV
running as production
running as development
running as prodution

questions.q: A request fails in production with an unexpected error. What should the client receive?
questions.explain: Stack traces, file paths and queries help an attacker and confuse users. In production the client gets a generic message, and you find the details in the logs by request id.
options: The full stack trace, so the user can report it
A generic error message; the details go only into the logs
The SQL query that failed
Nothing at all: close the connection

questions.q: Which rule does the lesson give for settings such as ports, URLs, secrets and feature switches?
questions.explain: One build, many environments. The code reads its settings from the environment; only the values change between your laptop, staging and production.
options: Put production values in the code and development values in .env
Everything that differs between environments comes from the environment, so the same build runs everywhere
Build a separate version of the app for each environment
Read them from a JSON file committed to git

questions.q: Why check all configuration at startup and list every problem at once?
questions.explain: Failing at startup means the deployment fails, not a customer's request. Listing every problem, not just the first, saves you a deploy for each missing value.
options: Because checking later is slower
So a missing value stops the app at once with a clear list, instead of failing at 3 a.m. on the first request that needs it
Because environment variables disappear after startup
So that secrets are printed where you can see them

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: "eighty" cannot become a number, and JWT_SECRET is missing. safeParse reports both problems, by path only, so you fix them in one go.
options: false [ 'PORT', 'JWT_SECRET' ]
false [ 'PORT' ]
false [ 'JWT_SECRET' ]
true

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A missing PORT falls back to its default and is a number. The program prints only the secret's length: a secret must never appear in output or logs.
options: 3000 number secret: 40 characters
3000 string secret: 40 characters
undefined undefined secret: 40 characters
3000 number secret: xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx

questions.q: Where should the real production database password live?
questions.explain: A local .env holds throwaway values and is never committed. On a server, the host provides secrets to the process, and only the app's user can read them.
options: In .env, committed so the whole team has it
In the source code, in a file called secrets.ts
In environment variables set by the host: a systemd EnvironmentFile readable only by the app's user, Docker secrets, or a secret manager
In the README, so the deployment steps are complete

questions.q: A developer who knew the production JWT secret leaves the company. What should you do?
questions.explain: Rotate whenever someone who knew a secret leaves, and at once if it may have leaked. Because the code reads it from the environment, rotating is a configuration change, not a code change.
options: Nothing, as long as they promise not to use it
Rotate it: replace it with a new secret in the host's environment; the code needs no change
Change the variable name in the code
Delete the secret and run without one

questions.q: Why should production logs be one line of JSON per event, with the same fields every time?
questions.explain: Nobody watches the terminal in production. A log tool searches millions of lines; that works when each event is structured the same way. Pretty output is for development.
options: JSON is shorter than plain text
Logs from every server go into one tool, which can filter by fields such as level or requestId
Terminals can only show JSON
JSON logs cannot contain secrets

questions.q: Where should the production app write its logs?
questions.explain: Writing to stdout keeps the app simple and lets the platform decide where logs go. The app should not manage log files itself.
options: Into a log file it rotates itself every night
To standard output; the process manager or Docker collects them
Into the database, in a logs table
Nowhere: logs slow the app down

questions.q: A tiny logger drops entries below its level. What does this print?
questions.explain: With level info, debug entries are dropped. Use INFO in production and switch one service to DEBUG for a while when hunting a bug. JSON.stringify prints double quotes, one line per entry.
options:
{"level":"info","msg":"task created"}
{"level":"error","msg":"database timeout"}
{"level":"error","msg":"database timeout"}

{ level: 'info', msg: 'task created' }
{ level: 'error', msg: 'database timeout' }

questions.q: This redacts field names that look secret before logging. What does it print?
questions.explain: The regular expression has the i flag and no anchors, so apiToken matches token too. Redaction is a safety net only: still never log request bodies whole.
options: {"requestId":"req-7","password":"[REDACTED]","apiToken":"[REDACTED]"}
{"requestId":"req-7","password":"[REDACTED]","apiToken":"abc"}
{"requestId":"[REDACTED]","password":"[REDACTED]","apiToken":"[REDACTED]"}
{"requestId":"req-7"}

questions.q: Which four "golden signals" does the lesson tell you to measure first?
questions.explain: How many requests, how many fail, how long they take, and how full your resources are. Together they tell you how the whole system is doing.
options: CPU, RAM, disk and network card
Traffic, errors, latency and saturation
Users, orders, revenue and refunds
Logs, traces, spans and events

questions.q: Nine requests are fast and one is slow. What does this print?
questions.explain: The mean of 60 ms describes none of the requests. p50 shows the typical request (14 ms) and p95 shows the slow tail your unluckiest users feel (480 ms). That is why latency is watched as percentiles.

questions.q: Why should the liveness check /health NOT check the database?
questions.explain: A failed liveness check means "restart me". Restarting cannot fix a database outage. Dependencies belong in the readiness check, which only stops traffic.
options: Database checks are too slow to write
If the database is down, the platform would restart every app server, which does not fix the database and only makes things worse
The database is checked by the browser instead
Liveness checks are not allowed to return JSON

questions.q: /ready answers 503 because the database is down. What should the platform do?
questions.explain: Readiness means "can I serve traffic right now?". When it fails, traffic goes to other servers. When the database comes back, the app becomes ready again by itself.
options: Restart the app at once
Stop sending it requests, without restarting it, until it is ready again
Delete the database and create a new one
Keep sending requests and let them fail

questions.q: Where does "the payment provider's API is reachable" belong?
questions.explain: Most pages still work without the payment provider. Taking the whole app out of traffic because one outside service is slow would turn a small problem into an outage.
options: Liveness, so the app restarts until the provider is back
Readiness, so the whole site stops getting traffic
Neither: handle it per request with a timeout and a clear error, and watch it with a metric
In the configuration check at startup

questions.q: Health endpoints are usually public. What should /ready return?
questions.explain: Versions, host names, connection strings and error messages help an attacker. Return a status; put the details in the logs.
options: The app version, the host name and the database connection string
The full error message from the failed check
Only a status, such as { ready: false }
A list of all environment variables

questions.q: What does this readiness endpoint answer?
questions.explain: Liveness says "alive" even while the database is down. Readiness needs every check to pass: one false makes it 503, and when the database comes back it answers 200 again.

questions.q: The platform sends SIGTERM during a deployment. What does a graceful shutdown do?
questions.explain: Without a graceful shutdown, every deployment cuts some customers' requests in half. The new requests are refused so a load balancer sends them elsewhere.
options: Exits at once so the new version can start faster
Stops accepting new requests, lets the ones in flight finish, closes resources such as the database pool, then exits
Ignores the signal and keeps running
Finishes new requests first, then old ones

questions.q: Docker waits 10 seconds after SIGTERM and then kills the process. How should you set gracefulShutdownTimeout?
questions.explain: If your timeout is longer than the platform's wait, the platform kills the process in the middle of shutdown, and the database pool and logs are not closed cleanly.
options: Longer than 10 seconds, so every request can finish
Shorter than the platform's wait, so shutdown finishes before the process is killed
To zero, so the process never waits
It does not matter: the platform always waits for the app

questions.q: This simulates a graceful shutdown. What does it print?
questions.explain: The new request is refused at once. The shutdown waits for the request already in flight, so order-1 finishes before closed, just like the lesson's HTTP example.
options:
SIGTERM: stop accepting
order-2: refused
order-1: done
closed

SIGTERM: stop accepting
closed
order-2: refused
order-1: done

order-1: done
SIGTERM: stop accepting
order-2: done
closed

SIGTERM: stop accepting
order-2: refused
closed
order-1: done

questions.q: What does SET statement_timeout = '5s' protect you from in PostgreSQL?
questions.explain: A timeout at every edge: incoming requests, outgoing calls and the database. A stuck query that is cancelled after 5 seconds frees its connection for other requests.
options: Slow network connections to the browser
One bad query holding a database connection for minutes
Too many login attempts
Running out of disk space

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The limiter counts per client. The first client gets 2 requests in the window and the third is refused. The second client has its own count, so it is allowed.
options: [ true, true, false, true ]
[ true, true, true, true ]
[ true, true, false, false ]
[ true, false, false, true ]

questions.q: Your app runs behind a reverse proxy and rate-limits by IP address. Everyone suddenly gets 429. What went wrong?
questions.explain: Behind a proxy the app sees the proxy's IP. Trust the forwarded client address only from the proxy you actually run; trusting it from anyone would let attackers pick any IP they like.
options: The limit is too high
Every request comes from the proxy's address, so all users share one bucket; set trustProxy to the proxy you run
Rate limiting does not work with HTTPS
The proxy blocks the Retry-After header

questions.q: This limiter counts by the address the app sees. Two different users come through the same proxy. What does it print?
questions.explain: Both users arrive from the proxy's address, so they share one counter and Bob is blocked by Ada's requests. The fix is to read the real client address from a proxy you trust.
options:
ada: true true
bob: false

ada: true true
bob: true

ada: true false
bob: true

ada: true true
bob: undefined

questions.q: You run four app servers, each with an in-memory rate limiter of 5 logins per minute. What is the real limit for one attacker?
questions.explain: An in-memory limiter counts per server. For a strict limit across servers, keep the counters in a shared store such as Redis.
options: 5 per minute, whichever server they reach
Up to 20 per minute, because each server counts on its own; keep the counters in Redis for a strict limit
1 per minute
No limit at all

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The second read comes from the cache, so it shows the old price. Only after invalidateByTag does the next read go to the database again. That is why every write must invalidate what it changed.
options: 12 12 10 queries: 2
12 10 10 queries: 3
12 12 12 queries: 1
12 10 10 queries: 2

questions.q: Every write already invalidates the cache. Why give every entry a TTL as well?
questions.explain: Sooner or later a code path forgets to invalidate. A TTL limits how long stale data can live. Also watch the hit rate: a cache that rarely hits costs memory for nothing.
options: TTLs make the cache faster
So a missed invalidation heals itself when the entry expires
So the cache never uses memory
Because tags do not work without a TTL

questions.q: EXPLAIN shows Seq Scan on orders with Filter: (customer_id = 42). What does it mean, and what is the usual fix?
questions.explain: A sequential scan reads every row. With an index, PostgreSQL looks the value up instead, which made the lesson's queries about ten times faster. Index the columns you filter, join and sort by often.
options: The query uses an index; nothing to do
PostgreSQL reads the whole table; add an index on customer_id if you filter by it often
The table is corrupted; restore a backup
The query has a syntax error

questions.q: This counts database queries for two ways of loading 10 orders with their customers. What does it print?
questions.explain: One query for the list plus one per item is the N+1 problem: 11 queries for 10 orders, and it grows with the list. WHERE id = ANY($1) or a join loads all customers in one query. (In real code, always pass values as parameters, never in the SQL text.)
options: one per item: 11 with ANY: 2
one per item: 10 with ANY: 2
one per item: 11 with ANY: 11
one per item: 1 with ANY: 2

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 90 connections are shared by 6 processes: 15 each. The background worker already uses 3 of them, so the web pool gets 12. Total connections = pool size × number of processes.
options: 15 12 true
16 13 true
15 12 false
90 87 true

questions.q: A pool has 2 connections and 3 queries start at once. What does this print?
questions.explain: Only two queries run at a time. The third waits in line and starts when a connection is handed back. Real pools such as the pg package's Pool work the same way.
options:
q1: running
q2: running
q3: waiting
q3: running

q1: running
q2: running
q3: running

q1: running
q2: waiting
q3: waiting
q2: running
q3: running

q3: waiting
q1: running
q2: running
q3: running

questions.q: Four app servers each have a database pool of 20. PostgreSQL allows 100 connections by default. What is the lesson's advice?
questions.explain: A database works best with a few busy connections. Small pools, a wait timeout so a full pool fails fast, and a pooler such as PgBouncer if deployments briefly double the number of processes.
options: Raise every pool to 100 to be safe
Remember that 4 × 20 = 80 is close to the limit; start small (about 10 per process) and set a wait timeout for getting a connection
Open a new connection for every query instead
Use one pool of 100 per server

questions.q: Finish checkEnv(env, required). Return a list of the names in required whose value is missing or an empty string. The program should print [ 'DATABASE_URL', 'JWT_SECRET' ] and then [].
questions.explain: Collect every missing name, not just the first, and report names only, never values. An empty string counts as missing, because !"" is true.

questions.q: Finish ready(checks). Each check is an async function that returns true or false. Run them all and return { status: 200, body: { ready: true } } when every check passed, otherwise { status: 503, body: { ready: false } }. The program should print 503 false and then 200 true.
questions.explain: Run the checks together with Promise.all and require all of them. The body is only a status: never put error messages or connection strings in a public health endpoint.

questions.q: Finish redact(meta). Return a new object where every key whose name contains password, secret or token (any case) has the value "[REDACTED]". Other values stay. The program should print {"requestId":"req-7","password":"[REDACTED]","JWT_SECRET":"[REDACTED]","taskId":42}.
questions.explain: The i flag makes the match ignore case, so JWT_SECRET is caught. Build a new object instead of changing the caller's one.

questions.q: Finish percentile(values, p) using the nearest-rank method: sort a copy of the numbers from small to large and return the item at index Math.ceil(p / 100 * length) - 1. The program should print p50: 14 p95: 480.
questions.explain: Sort with (a, b) => a - b: the default sort() compares numbers as text. Copy first with [...values] so the caller's array is not changed.

questions.q: Finish check(ip, now) for a fixed-window rate limiter: at most max requests per client in each window of windowMs. Keep, per ip, the window's start time and a count; start a new window when now - start >= windowMs. Return true when the request is allowed. The program should print [ true, true, true, false, true ].
questions.explain: The fourth login attempt inside the minute is refused (in an app, a 429 with Retry-After). At 61 s a new window starts. The time is passed in, so the result is the same on every run.

questions.q: Finish webPoolSize({ limit, reserved, processes, workerPool }). Share limit - reserved connections equally between the processes (round down), then subtract the worker's pool. The program should print 12 and 20.
questions.explain: Math.floor rounds down, because you can never use part of a connection, and rounding up would exceed the limit. 90 / 4 = 22.5 → 22, minus 2 for the worker.

questions.q: The product cache shows a stale price after an update. Finish updatePrice(sku, price): change the price in db, then invalidate the products tag. The program should print 12 and then 10.
questions.explain: Write first, then invalidate. The next read misses the cache and loads the new price. Forgetting the invalidation is the classic caching bug: customers see the old price until the TTL runs out.

questions.q: This loader reports every problem by name. What does it print?
questions.explain: The loader collects all problems before it throws, so you fix everything in one deploy. The message names the settings and never shows their values, so a nearly-right secret cannot leak through a log.
options:
Invalid configuration:
  PORT: must be a whole number
  JWT_SECRET: at least 32 characters

Invalid configuration:
  PORT: must be a whole number

Invalid configuration:
  PORT: eighty
  JWT_SECRET: hunter2
{ port: NaN }

questions.q: Every outgoing call gets a time limit. What does this print?
questions.explain: The fast query wins the race. The slow one loses to the 30 ms timer, so the caller stops waiting instead of holding memory and a connection. clearTimeout in finally cleans up the timer either way.
options:
fast rows
slow timed out after 30 ms

fast rows
slow rows

fast timed out after 30 ms
slow timed out after 30 ms

slow timed out after 30 ms
fast rows
